Revenue growth

Cyclical industries such as energy can make mediocre companies look strong for a time, but a long-term view reveals which businesses can actually withstand and adapt to changing conditions. Devon Energy’s revenue grew at an impressive 17.6% compounded annual growth rate over the last five years. Its growth surpassed the average energy upstream and integrated energy company and shows its offerings resonate with customers.

Even a long stretch in energy can be shaped by a single commodity cycle, so extending the view to ten years adds another perspective and reveals which companies are built to grow regardless of the pricing regime. Devon Energy’s annualized revenue growth of 8.5% over the last ten years is below its five-year trend, but the results still suggest decent demand.

While looking at revenue is important, it can also introduce noise around commodity prices and mergers and acquisitions. Analyzing drivers of revenue, on the other hand, highlights what is happening inside the asset base and whether the economic footprint of a company is expanding. Over the last two years, Devon Energy’s oil production per day averaged 30.8% year-on-year growth while its natural gas production per day averaged 26.8% year-on-year growth.

Adjusted EBITDA margin

Devon Energy has been an efficient company over the last five years. It was one of the more profitable businesses in the energy upstream and integrated energy sector, with an average EBITDA margin of 47.7%.

Analyzing the trend in its profitability, Devon Energy’s EBITDA margin decreased by 5.4 percentage points over the last year. This raises questions about the company’s expense base because its revenue growth should have given it leverage on its fixed costs, resulting in better economies of scale and profitability.

Key takeaways from Devon Energy’s Q3 results
Devon Energy’s revenue miss left room for improvement this quarter, despite EPS beating analysts’ consensus estimates. Shares fell 4.2% to $42.01 immediately after the report.

Devon Energy may have had a tough quarter, but does that create an investment opportunity? What happened in the latest quarter matters, but not as much as longer-term business quality and valuation when deciding whether to invest in this stock.
